decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker: “paste a web address; the app records it”; Round 1 client: “I approve the specification.” Round 4 maker again reports URL-based saving.
decisions.note: The presented save-by-URL behavior conforms to the reference. Specification and implementation stages.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker specifies only “auto-fills the page title”; Round 2 says “Best-effort title fetch”; Round 4 reports only “auto-fetches the title when blank.” Clients respond with approval or final acceptance without mentioning the missing description, favicon, or preview image.
decisions.note: The metadata decision collects only the title, while the reference requires title, description, favicon, and preview image. The repeated approvals are bare approvals, so the divergence remained unexpressed across specification, planning, and implementation review.

decisions.evidence: Round 2 maker: “when you don't type a title” and Round 1 maker: “fix a title/address”; no editable auto-collected description is presented. Round 1 and Round 2 clients approve without identifying that difference.
decisions.note: Title entry/editing is presented before and after saving, but description collection and editing are absent from the stated metadata model. Specification and planning stages.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker defines editing as “fix a title/address”; Round 4 summarizes delivery only as “edit form.” The client approves the specification and later accepts the application without requesting editing of description, tags, and note.
decisions.note: The expressly presented edit scope is narrower than the required URL/title/description/tags/note editing. Specification through implementation review.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker: “remove a bookmark (with a confirm step)”; Round 4 maker: “delete with a required confirmation.” The corresponding clients approve and accept.
decisions.note: Deletion is supported; the added confirmation step does not conflict with the reference. Specification and implementation stages.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker commits to a “duplicate warning”; Round 2 says it “warns ... when you re-save the same address”; Round 4 makes the behavior explicit as “warns on duplicates (with ‘save anyway’).” Round 4 client only says the application meets the approved behavior and accepts it.
decisions.note: Allowing “save anyway” permits duplicate creation instead of converging on editing the existing bookmark. The evolving duplicate-handling decision is counted once; no client response expresses the reference expectation. Specification through implementation review.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker says only “see everything you've saved”; Rounds 3–4 describe a “newest-first list” but do not state which fields each item exposes or establish readability-first presentation. Client approvals provide no clarification.
decisions.note: A bookmark list is presented, but the record cannot establish whether every item exposes title, description, tags, and favicon as required. The decision remains unresolved through implementation review.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker: “click through to the original page”; Round 4 maker: “opens in a new tab.” Clients approve and accept.
decisions.note: Opening the original URL in a new tab is functionally equivalent to the required navigation. Specification and implementation stages.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker: “Tags are included ... per bookmark,” alongside notes as bookmark fields; Round 1 client approves the specification and assumptions.
decisions.note: The presentation records per-bookmark tag support, consistent with assigning one or more tags. Specification stage.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker: “filter by tag”; Round 4 maker reports “tag filter.” Clients approve and accept.
decisions.note: Filtering bookmarks by a selected tag conforms to the reference. Specification through implementation review.

decisions.evidence: Round 4 maker defines the delivered scope as “live search over title/address/notes/tags,” omitting description from the enumerated searchable fields. Round 4 client responds only: “This meets the approved behavior.”
decisions.note: The implemented search field set omits description, which the reference requires alongside title, note, and URL. The final approval does not state or accept that difference explicitly. Implementation review.

decisions.evidence: Round 3 maker presents “List newest-first”; Round 4 again reports a “newest-first list.” Neither presentation says whether the user can choose another sort key, and the client does not clarify.
decisions.note: Newest-first may be only a default or may be fixed; the record cannot establish whether user-selectable sorting exists. Planning and implementation stages.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker says “notes are a free-text field per bookmark”; later presentations mention searching notes but do not say whether Markdown is rendered. Round 1 approval and final acceptance do not clarify this.
decisions.note: A free-text input can hold Markdown source, so the wording alone does not establish either conformance or divergence on Markdown rendering. Specification through implementation review.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker assumption 4: “No import/export from browsers or files in v1.” Round 1 client: “I approve the specification and the five assumptions.”
decisions.note: The explicit exclusion removes Netscape HTML import. Referencing approval of all assumptions is still bare approval and does not express the expected feature or difference. Specification gate.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker assumption 4: “No import/export from browsers or files in v1.” Round 1 client: “I approve the specification and the five assumptions.”
decisions.note: The explicit exclusion removes Netscape HTML export. Import and export are separable reference requirements; the client does not independently state or accept the difference. Specification gate.
